system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-06-11 20:35:00 to 2184-06-14 14:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma and a history of biliary stents and recurrent infections, was admitted with fever, chills, and lack of output from his percutaneous biliary drain, consistent with cholangitis and early sepsis. On admission, he underwent percutaneous balloon dilation and exchange of his biliary drain. Blood cultures grew E. coli, prompting a switch to IV meropenem. An MRCP showed signs of cholangitis and biliary stenosis, leading to an ERCP for clearance of sludge and debris from the stents. His biliary drain was subsequently capped, and he improved clinically with normalized liver enzymes and resolution of fever. He was diagnosed with bacteremia and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, managed with insulin and diet. He was discharged home with a plan for 10 days of IV meropenem via home health, prophylactic oral vancomycin, and follow-up for liver tests and oncology care.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, not intractable, without status migrainosus
Benign prostatic hyperplasia without lower urinary tract symptoms
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other organs and systems
Calculus of bile duct without cholangitis or cholecystitis without obstruction

25 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service

PROCEDURE:
1. Cholangiogram through existing  percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
access.
2. Exchange of the existing percutaneous trans-hepatic biliary drainage
catheter with a new 8 ___ modified the strong internal/external PTBD
catheter.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The right abdomen was prepped and draped in the usual sterile
fashion.
Initial scout images showed biliary drain in the appropriate position. The
right tube was injected with dilute contrast.  The percutaneous
cholecystostomy tube was also injected with diluted contrast.  The images were
stored on PACS.
Following the subcutaneous injection of 1% lidocaine and instillation of
lidocaine jelly into the skin site, the right catheter was cut and ___
wire was advanced through the catheter into the duodenum.  The catheter was
removed over the wire and a 8 ___ percutaneous trans hepatic biliary
drainage catheter was advanced into the duodenum. The wire and inner stiffener
were removed, the catheter was flushed attached to a bag and sterile dressings
were applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
post-procedure complications.

FINDINGS:


1. Patent percutaneous cholecystostomy tube.
2. Cholangiogram showing obstruction of the distal segment of the internal/
external PTBD.
3. Successful exchange of existing percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
catheters with new 8 ___ PTBD.

catheters with new 8 ___ PTBD.  Catheters were attached to a bag for

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in today with nausea and a low-grade fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I woke up feeling queasy, had chills, and my temperature was 99. I called my oncologist and he told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. I see you have two biliary drains—one capped and one that usually drains into a bag. How much output do you normally get?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About 30 to 40 cc a day from the one on gravity. But today—nothing. I opened the other one too, just in case, and that’s dry as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. No output could mean a blockage. You also mentioned some right upper quadrant pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little, especially when I cough. But it’s not sharp or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ve checked your labs and your bilirubin is elevated. That, plus the fever and no drain output, makes us worry about a biliary obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? But I just finished antibiotics a few weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Given your history of cholangitis and E. coli bacteremia, we’ve started you on IV meropenem just in case. But we need to find out if the tube is blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get a chest X-ray to make sure there’s no infection in your lungs, and then tomorrow morning, interventional radiology will do a cholangiogram to look at the drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And if it’s blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They may replace the tube. It’s a common procedure for patients like you. We’ll keep you on antibiotics until we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your liver enzymes are up—alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are elevated. That supports the idea of a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just in my head. I knew something was off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. The radiology team is reviewing your case now. You’re scheduled for a cholangiogram this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the procedure is done. They found a blockage in the distal part of your PTBD tube. It was completely obstructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So that’s why nothing was coming out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They removed the old tube and put in a new 8 French PTBD catheter. It’s now draining into a bag.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same kind of tube I had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same type but fresh. The old one likely got clogged with sludge or debris. This should fix the flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? Do I still need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on infectious disease to weigh in. Since your blood cultures are negative and you don’t have signs of active infection, they may stop them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Update: ID agrees. No signs of cholangitis—your fever’s gone, labs are stable. They don’t think you need more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m off the IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discontinue the meropenem. Your symptoms were likely from the blockage, not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about another round of sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. But you’re not showing signs of that now. Your drain is working, and your liver numbers should start to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your bilirubin dropped from 1.6 to 0.4 today. That’s a great sign the new tube is doing its job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel better too—no nausea, no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re going to cap the drain later today to see if you tolerate it, just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We capped the PTBD an hour ago. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. No discomfort at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep it capped overnight. If you stay symptom-free, we can discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? That’d be nice. But what about the drain care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home health will visit you twice a week to check the site and manage the drain. You’ll also have a nurse teach you some basics before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made it through the night with the drain capped—no issues. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting. Keep the site clean and dry. Call us if you develop fever, pain, or the drain stops working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with him in a week. Your cancer is still being monitored, but no treatment changes now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my platelets? They’ve been low for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your platelet count is 81, which is low but stable for you. No intervention needed unless it drops further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’ll send all instructions with you, and home health will be at your house tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ll keep an eye on things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You know your body best. Call us at the first sign of trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma and a history of biliary drains, was readmitted with nausea, chills, and absence of biliary drain output. He was initially treated with IV meropenem for suspected cholangitis. A cholangiogram revealed obstruction of the distal PTBD catheter, which was successfully replaced percutaneously. Post-procedure, his symptoms resolved, liver enzymes improved, and blood cultures remained negative. Infectious disease determined antibiotics were unnecessary, as the presentation was consistent with mechanical obstruction rather than infection. The drain was capped without complications, and he was discharged home with home health support for drain care. His thrombocytopenia remained stable, and oncology follow-up was arranged.
